what_its_for: Bisoprolol is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and heart failure. It helps your heart beat more slowly and with less force, which lowers your blood pressure and reduces the work your heart has to do. This can help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and kidney problems.
how_to_take: Take bisoprolol by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or split it unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay. Try to take it at the same time every day, which helps keep the medicine working steadily in your body. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious heart problems.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take. The usual starting dose for adults is 2.5 mg to 5 mg once a day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose up to 10 mg or 20 mg once a day depending on your condition and how well you respond to the medicine. Always follow your doctor's instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store bisoprolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the medicine in its original container with the cap tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking bisoprolol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and make you feel dizzy or faint. Do not take over-the-counter cold, allergy, or diet medicines without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first, as some of these can raise your blood pressure or interfere with bisoprolol. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can make you feel dizzy. Be careful when driving or using machinery until you know how this medicine affects you.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: very slow heartbeat (fewer than 60 beats per minute), severe dizziness or fainting, shortness of breath or wheezing, sudden weight gain of more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week, swelling in your legs or ankles, chest pain, cold or bluish hands and feet, or signs of low blood sugar if you are diabetic (since bisoprolol can hide some of these warning signs). Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Bisoprolol starts lowering your heart rate and blood pressure within a few hours of your first dose. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks before you feel the full benefit for blood pressure, and it may take several weeks to months for the full benefit in heart failure. Even if you feel well, keep taking your medicine every day — high blood pressure often has no symptoms, and stopping the medicine can cause your condition to get worse.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the side effects of bisoprolol, especially dizziness. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if your kidneys or liver are not working well. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Bisoprolol may not be safe during pregnancy and can pass into breast milk. Diabetes: This medicine may hide some signs of low blood sugar (like a fast heartbeat). Check your blood sugar regularly and tell your doctor if you notice any changes. Asthma or breathing problems: Bisoprolol may worsen breathing problems. Tell your doctor if you have asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
